claims.statement: The service has two equivalent entrypoints — the installed console script `haap-dird` (`haap_directory.cli:main`) and the source launcher `python haap_dird.py`, which inserts `src` on sys.path and calls the same `cli.main()`; Python >= 3.10 is required and `cryptography` is the only hard runtime dependency.

`haap-dird` serves by default (binding a stdlib ThreadingHTTPServer on config.host:config.port, default 0.0.0.0:8444, plain HTTP) and offers offline actions `--prune` (opens the store, prunes expired entries, prints the count, exits; needs no key) and `--gen-key` (loads or mints the directory key, prints directory_fingerprint and key_path, exits without binding); CLI overrides are limited to the six fields db_path, host, port, ttl_hours, max_agents, key_path.

Configuration precedence is CLI flags > config file > env HAAP_DIRD_* > built-in defaults, implemented by DirectoryConfig.load applying env, then the JSON config file, then CLI overrides, with each value coerced to the type of the dataclass default; the config file path resolves from --config, else HAAP_DIRD_CONFIG, else ~/.haap/dird.json.

Environment variables follow HAAP_DIRD_<UPPER_DATACLASS_FIELD>, booleans accept 1/true/yes/on, and invalid scalar values (e.g. non-numeric HAAP_DIRD_PORT) raise at DirectoryConfig.load time so configuration errors fail fast at process start rather than at request time.

A missing, unparseable, or non-dict config file is silently treated as empty ({}), so a corrupt dird.json quietly yields defaults; list-typed fields such as moderator_keys pass _coerce unvalidated, so they must be set via the JSON config file — an env-provided string would reach ModerationService as a string and silently produce no valid moderators.

The DirectoryConfig carries the full operational field set with defaults: serve (db_path 'dird.db', host '0.0.0.0', port 8444, ttl_hours 24.0, max_agents 10000, key_path '', trust_proxy_headers false), size/limits (challenge_ttl_s 120, max_pending_challenges 5000, max_manifest_bytes 256 KiB, max_body_bytes 512 KiB), rate limits (rate_search_per_min 60, rate_register_per_hour 5), L2 timers (domain_token_ttl_s 1800, domain_verification_ttl_days 90, max_pending_verifications 5), L3/L4 reputation thresholds, checkpoint_interval_s 3600, and moderator_keys as a list of base64 Ed25519 public keys; the directory signing key is never part of this config object.

The directory key is managed by keystore.load_or_create_key at config.resolved_key_path() — key_path if set, else `<db>.dirkey.json` via os.path.splitext(abspath(db_path)) — minted on first use, written atomically (tmp file + os.replace) with 0600 permissions, in JSON format haap-directory-key-v1 carrying fingerprint/public_key/private_key, and load rejects any other format marker.

The key fingerprint is the directory_fingerprint: 'HF-' plus the first 16 hex characters of sha256 of the raw 32-byte public key; it is surfaced by /health, embedded in search/profile responses, and echoed as X-HAAP-Directory-Fingerprint on signed audit responses.

The directory key signs the legacy registration challenge nonce, L5 audit checkpoints (Ed25519 over the canonical JSON of {seq, entry_hash, ts} at the chain head), and every /v1/audit/* response body (X-HAAP-Directory-Signature over canonical JSON of the body); haap-dird --gen-key prints the fingerprint and key path for identity publication.

Startup order: Store connects with PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL, foreign_keys=ON and busy_timeout=5000, creates the schema idempotently and ensures the genesis audit entry (seq 0, chain.genesis); DirectoryService prunes expired entries on startup; DirectoryHTTPServer binds and starts a background checkpoint thread calling audit.maybe_checkpoint every max(1, checkpoint_interval_s) seconds; live-agent reads prune lazily so stale listings are never observed.

Graceful shutdown: cli.main installs SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that call server.stop(); stop() sets the stop event, shuts the HTTP socket down, signs one final L5 audit checkpoint (best effort), then closes the store; there is no explicit PRAGMA wal_checkpoint anywhere, so a clean stop relies on SQLite checkpointing the WAL when the last connection closes, and a SIGKILL leaves committed transactions in -wal/-shm files that SQLite replays at next open.

GET /health returns {status, version, protocol_version, agents (live count), suspended, chain_seq (audit head seq), uptime_s, directory_fingerprint, api.completion_route} with no sensitive data; pending_verifications is always hard-coded 0 rather than computed — a divergence from the field list implied by docs/OPERATE.md.

GET /metrics serves Prometheus text exposition (Content-Type text/plain; version=0.0.4) with gauges/counters haapd_agents_listed, haapd_agents_suspended, haapd_agents_total (all agent rows including history), haapd_audit_seq, haapd_ops_total (all handled requests), haapd_uptime_seconds, and haapd_rejections_total labeled by stable error code such as code="RATE_LIMITED".

Every response carries X-Request-Id (the client-supplied value echoed, else generated req_<hex>); rejections use the stable envelope {"error": {code, message, request_id}} with the code-to-HTTP table in errors.py; 429 responses carry Retry-After in whole seconds, and any unexpected handler exception is converted to INTERNAL_ERROR (500) so internals never reach the wire.

Anonymous per-IP token-bucket rate limiting protects search (capacity rate_search_per_min, default 60, refill over 60 s) and register/verify-domain (capacity rate_register_per_hour, default 5, refill over 3600 s); buckets refill continuously, denials are 429 RATE_LIMITED with whole-second Retry-After, and the limiters are in-memory per process, so they reset on restart and multi-instance deployments need a shared limiter or WAF in front.

The rate-limit key is the TCP peer address unless trust_proxy_headers is enabled and the TCP peer is loopback (127.0.0.1 or ::1), in which case CF-Connecting-IP or the first X-Forwarded-For entry is used; forwarding headers from any non-loopback peer are ignored because they are spoofable.

Payload and capacity abuse controls: request bodies larger than max_body_bytes (512 KiB default) are rejected PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE (413) from the Content-Length header before reading; canonical manifests larger than max_manifest_bytes (256 KiB default) are rejected MANIFEST_TOO_LARGE (413); a registration for a fingerprint not currently live is refused DIRECTORY_FULL (503) when count_live() >= max_agents, while a live fingerprint re-registering is exempt.

Endpoint challenges share a global pending cap max_pending_challenges (default 5000): an insert beyond the cap evicts the oldest pending challenge by created_epoch and appends an audited challenge.evicted entry in the same transaction; domain challenges are capped per agent at max_pending_verifications (default 5) with VERIFICATION_LIMIT_REACHED; all challenges are single-use with short TTLs.

L2 domain-control checks are performed by the directory itself through an injectable resolver seam: the dns_txt method shells out to the system dig binary (bind9-dnsutils / Debian dnsutils; 10 s timeout) resolving TXT _haap.<domain> and rejects off-registrable-domain CNAME answers, while a missing or failing dig surfaces as DNS_ERROR_TEMPORARY (503); the https_well_known method uses only the stdlib, follows redirects only within the same registrable domain, caps the response at 4 KiB and times out at 10 s.

Confirmed domain verifications last domain_verification_ttl_days (default 90) and require the verified domain to cover the manifest endpoint host (DOMAIN_ENDPOINT_MISMATCH otherwise); expired verification rows are filtered out rather than deleted, and domain_verified is a control signal with provenance, never 'verified business' or KYC.

Moderators are operator-held Ed25519 keys whose base64 public keys are configured as moderator_keys: ModerationService derives each fingerprint at startup (malformed entries skipped), rejects unknown fingerprints with MODERATOR_UNKNOWN (403) and bad signatures with TAKEDOWN_UNAUTHORIZED (403), and every moderator action (takedown, suspend, unsuspend) plus the automated auto-suspend is recorded on the L5 audit chain with the moderator fingerprint.

Because the L5 audit entry is appended inside the same BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction as the state change it records, sqlite3 dird.db ".backup ..." yields a consistent online snapshot of both state and chain; restore is stop the service, replace dird.db (WAL checkpointed after a clean stop), restore the separate .dirkey.json key file, and restart — startup then prunes entries that expired while offline with audited agent.expired transitions.

The Docker image builds from python:3.11-slim with dnsutils installed for dig, installs the package, and runs haap-dird as non-root user haap with uid 10001; ENV HAAP_DIRD_DB_PATH=/data/dird.db with matching CMD flags puts both the SQLite DB and the derived key file /data/dird.dirkey.json on the /data volume, so recreating the container without a persistent volume mints a new key and a new directory_fingerprint.

Trust boundaries an operator must communicate: the directory verifies signatures, fingerprint-key binding and endpoint control but returns labelled signals with provenance and never a trust verdict; a hostile operator can lie about listings but cannot sign as an agent, so consumers must re-verify an agent's own /.well-known/haap.json against the listing fingerprint; the audit chain is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof — rewrites are detectable only by parties holding a signed checkpoint fetched before the rewrite or running an independent mirror, so consumers should poll /v1/audit/head and verify signed responses.
